salient-trial: The moment of truth in a supermarket rarely feels momentous. A shopper moves between familiar brands, compares prices, and clicks 'add to basket'. Yet those countless small decisions shape agriculture, emissions, land use and the environmental footprint of the food system. If researchers want to help people eat more sustainably, the online supermarket is an unusually revealing place to look.

A 2026 working paper, *Effects of Eco-labels and Price Discounts on Promoting More Sustainable Grocery Purchases in an Online UK Supermarket: A Randomised Controlled Field Trial*, examines two candidate levers: information about environmental impacts and the prices customers actually face. The central question is simple to pose and much harder to answer: are people more willing to choose greener groceries when they know which products are better, when greener alternatives cost less, or when both changes occur together?

Why study this in a real shopping environment? Surveys can capture concern about the climate; hypothetical choices can reveal stated preferences. Neither necessarily predicts what happens when someone is buying dinner after a long day. A field experiment puts the question nearer to the decision itself, where habits, budget constraints, brands and convenience compete for attention. That distinction is central to understanding why expressed environmental values do not always turn into greener baskets.

Eco-labels try to solve an information problem. Even motivated customers rarely know the relative environmental impacts of two similar products. A clear, comparable indicator can make those differences visible at the point of purchase. But attention is scarce in a crowded interface. Shoppers may not notice a label, may find it hard to interpret, or may treat other attributes as more important. Offering information is not the same thing as changing behaviour.

Discounts operate through a different mechanism: they change the immediate trade-off. A small price difference can matter, especially when consumers are purchasing multiple items and working within a household budget. Price incentives may also make environmental information more salient, drawing the shopper's eye to an alternative that would otherwise be ignored. Studying the two together lets researchers ask whether information and financial incentives reinforce one another.

The experiment's setting matters almost as much as its intervention. Online food shopping produces a sequence of observable product choices and offers the possibility of integrating research into everyday digital platforms. That makes it a promising laboratory for practical policy—but also brings challenges. The shopper's previous habits, the structure of product listings, what alternatives are available and how smoothly an intervention appears on screen may all influence the outcome.

The broader stakes extend beyond choosing a favourite kind of eco-label. If price incentives work where labels alone do not, it strengthens the case for examining the relative prices of sustainable and less sustainable foods. If labels help identify attractive substitutions, their value may be in improving search and comparison rather than directly persuading everyone to change. These interpretations should be evaluated against the paper's reported estimates and uncertainty, not inferred from the title alone.

The useful lesson is methodological as well as practical: sustainable eating can be investigated as a series of real trade-offs rather than a test of consumers' good intentions. The working paper provides a basis for discussing how digital food environments might be redesigned, while leaving crucial implementation questions for future research: how durable are any changes, who benefits, how do effects vary across households, and what would happen at scale? The original paper is linked below for its precise results and design.
food-policy-review: When governments try to improve diets, there is a bewildering menu of possible interventions. They can tax sugary drinks, subsidise healthier foods, require labels, change the products companies manufacture or alter the food available in public institutions. What they cannot do is assume that every attractive idea delivers the same health benefit for the same cost.

A 2025 paper in *Frontiers in Nutrition*, *Health economics evidence for food system policy: a systematic review of reviews*, steps back from individual interventions to examine the research landscape. Instead of evaluating one tax or one labelling programme, the researchers synthesised 36 existing reviews covering 718 primary studies. Their aim was not merely to ask whether interventions work, but to map where economic evidence exists, what methods researchers have used and where the blind spots lie.

One striking finding concerns what the research community has chosen to study. Twenty-one of the reviews concentrated on policies influencing consumer demand, such as taxes, subsidies and information. Only four looked exclusively at interventions on the supply side, while another eleven spanned both. The imbalance matters because a food system is not just a collection of individual choices. Manufacturers, retailers and public authorities determine which products are offered, their composition, their prices and how they are presented.

Within the evidence brought together, supply-side measures—reformulation is an example—appeared more effective at altering dietary behaviours than demand-side approaches such as labels. That should not be read as a universal ranking of every possible reformulation policy against every possible tax or subsidy. The underlying interventions and contexts differ. Still, it challenges the assumption that better consumer information alone is enough to transform a population's diet.

Consider reformulation. If a manufacturer reduces the salt in a widely consumed product, the composition of many meals can change without every customer making a deliberate decision. A label, by contrast, requires attention, comprehension, motivation and an opportunity to act. That difference helps explain why changing the environment in which choices are made can be powerful. It also raises questions about what reformulation may cost, whether firms pass costs to consumers and how the benefits are distributed.

The paper makes another important observation: methods vary dramatically. Researchers evaluating potential supply-side policies have often relied on ex-ante estimates—modelling what might happen before an intervention occurs. Demand-side studies mix such projections with ex-post evaluations of real policies. As a result, directly comparing cost-effectiveness figures across reviews is difficult. A finding derived from a model is not interchangeable with a result observed after a policy was introduced.

That is why the authors advocate looking at costs and benefits from a societal perspective. A policy may impose costs on firms or consumers while creating benefits through better health, reduced healthcare spending or improved productivity. An accounting exercise focused narrowly on one budget can miss most of those consequences. The distribution of costs and gains matters too: what is good on average might be experienced very differently by households with different incomes.

Perhaps the most practical implication is that policymakers should think in combinations rather than isolated interventions. A label may help some shoppers; product reformulation could change what everyone consumes; price changes may shift demand in other ways. Their interactions are an empirical question, not something to presume. Future research needs credible evaluations that compare packages of measures, investigate real economic effects and identify who gains.

This review does not hand policymakers one magic instrument. It offers something more useful: an evidence map showing how much of the policy conversation has focused on consumers, how much remains to be learned about suppliers, and why better economic evaluation is essential before calling any food-system intervention a success.
wage-rigidity: Why don't wages fall when the economy turns sour? For generations, economists have treated this as one of the labour market's central puzzles. If employers are reluctant to cut nominal pay, then economic downturns may lead to job losses instead of smaller wage packets. Such wage rigidity plays a major role in how economists think about unemployment, inflation and the transmission of monetary policy.

The puzzle has an unmistakable visual signature. When researchers plot year-to-year changes in individual wages from household surveys, they often find an unusually large pile-up at exactly zero. Rather than reporting a small pay rise or cut, many workers appear to have received precisely the same nominal wage as the previous year. That spike has become familiar evidence of downward nominal wage rigidity and wage stickiness more generally.

But a 2025 Warwick working paper asks whether the spike might partly be a trick of measurement. In *Why did we think wages are rigid for all those years?*, See-Yu Chan, Stephan Hobler and Thijs van Rens revisit US Current Population Survey data and examine what happens when workers round the wages they report. Their argument starts with a mundane observation: when asked about earnings, people do not always provide an exact figure to the penny.

Imagine someone earns an hourly wage that moves from a value slightly below a round number to one slightly above it. If both responses are rounded to the same convenient figure, a genuine pay change can disappear in the survey. A researcher then sees a zero change where the pay records would show movement. Even fairly ordinary reporting practices can distort the shape of the entire wage-change distribution, especially at a single point like zero.

The quantitative effect is substantial. The paper reports that adjusting for potential rounding reduces the share of apparent zero changes from roughly 15–20 per cent to about 7–12 per cent. The corrected figures align much more closely with estimates from recent administrative-data studies. In other words, nominal wage rigidity does not vanish; the amount implied by raw survey data looks considerably smaller once measurement is considered.

That nuance is crucial. The paper is not claiming that employers freely adjust wages every month or that nominal pay cuts are commonplace. It is challenging the inference that the uncorrected spike measures rigid wages accurately. A statistical feature of household survey answers may have been interpreted for years as a feature of wage-setting behaviour. Correcting that feature changes the scale of the phenomenon economists are trying to explain.

This is a reminder that economic data are constructed, not discovered in pristine form. Surveys ask questions; respondents interpret them; numbers are remembered or rounded; researchers clean and compare them. Each step can affect what the final graph appears to say. Even patterns repeated in influential papers deserve a second look when their generating process is not fully understood.

The wider implications reach into macroeconomics. Models that use evidence about wage inflexibility to explain unemployment dynamics, adjustment to shocks or the persistence of inflation rely on the magnitude of the underlying rigidity. If a portion of the measured rigidity comes from reporting, calibrations and interpretations may need revisiting. The paper does not by itself settle which models are right, but it sharpens the empirical target they need to match.

The most compelling part of the story may be its simplicity: a longstanding debate about wage-setting can turn on a very human habit of saying 'about twenty pounds' instead of giving a more exact number. The working paper illustrates how much can change when economists scrutinise the measurement behind a familiar fact.
pilot-online-groceries: Imagine studying grocery choices inside a supermarket without needing the supermarket itself to run the experiment. That is the unusual prospect explored by a 2025 pilot study published in *BMC Research Notes*. Rather than redesigning a retailer's website, the researchers built a browser extension that could add environmental information while volunteers shopped on an existing UK online supermarket site.

The question was timely. Food production has important environmental consequences, yet shoppers face a difficult information problem: sustainability is rarely obvious from packaging, brand or price. An eco-label can make environmental differences visible. But does such a label change the products people actually buy, and can it be tested during routine shopping rather than in a simulated online store?

The pilot, *Promoting environmentally sustainable food purchases in online grocery shopping: insights from a pilot randomised controlled field trial*, was designed primarily to test whether this style of experiment could be run and what a larger study would need. That distinction matters. A small feasibility trial should not be judged as though it were a definitive answer to the effectiveness of eco-labels.

The team screened 504 people and found 161 eligible to take part. Of those, 57 downloaded the extension: 23 allocated to the control group and 34 to the intervention group. Just 22 shopped at least once during the one-month trial. Those numbers convey the core operational challenge. Recruiting interested people is not the same as getting software installed, functioning and used during a real grocery order.

Among the shoppers observed, the average environmental score of purchased items was not statistically different between groups. The reported means were 32 in the control group and 41 in the intervention group, with a p-value of 0.22. That is not evidence of a meaningful improvement from eco-labels in this small sample. But with so few participants making purchases, the study could not reliably detect modest effects.

The follow-up feedback tells an equally important story. Sixty-nine eligible participants completed a survey and highlighted practical changes that could improve a future trial: more technical support, clearer information about labels, reminders and stronger incentives. Such details can sound unglamorous, yet they determine whether a digital intervention survives contact with ordinary life. A tool that is confusing or difficult to install cannot influence choices, however appealing its theory.

The study's methodological innovation is worth dwelling on. Browser extensions could allow independent researchers to test changes to the information customers see without negotiating full technological integration with a supermarket chain. That may open the door to more rapid and transparent experiments across real shopping environments. It also creates its own constraints: browser compatibility, user consent, privacy, technical stability and the limits of what a third-party extension can observe.

The pilot therefore produced a mixed but useful answer. It did not show that adding eco-labels made baskets more sustainable. It did show that a live shopping experiment of this sort is possible, and it identified the technical and recruitment problems a larger trial needs to solve. The main trial, registered as ISRCTN18800054, was intended to pursue those questions at greater scale.

For food policy, that distinction between 'did the intervention work?' and 'can we measure whether it works?' is easy to overlook. Before governments or businesses bet on the latest digital nudge, researchers need rigorous ways to observe behaviour in the real world. This pilot helps build that infrastructure—even if its initial environmental labels were not a demonstrated success.
pantry-food-insecurity: Food insecurity can be described in national percentages, but it is experienced much more personally: in shopping decisions, skipped meals and anxiety over what a household will eat next. Community food pantries try to change that experience without following the conventional food-bank model. Members pay a fee and gain access to a selection of groceries. The question is whether that kind of arrangement makes a measurable difference, rather than simply offering a welcome service.

A research team examined the Your Local Pantry network in England using a quasi-experimental study. Instead of comparing pantry members with an entirely different group of households, the researchers recruited people who were applying for membership. Some acquired and used memberships; others had membership but did not use it; and some were placed on waiting lists because particular pantries were oversubscribed. That variation provided a potentially informative comparison, although it was not the same as a randomised trial.

The researchers recruited participants between February and August 2025, collecting information at the beginning and then again after two, six and ten weeks. Their main outcome was food insecurity, assessed using a validated eight-item measure developed by the US Department of Agriculture. This measures experiences of difficulty getting enough food, rather than merely asking how much money respondents spend on groceries.

In total, 216 people from 83 pantries took part. The participants were disproportionately women, and just over half reported having children. Forty per cent reported monthly earnings of £1,000 or less. The baseline numbers indicate substantial need: 83 per cent were already experiencing moderate or severe food insecurity. The study therefore assessed an intervention among people for whom food access was far from an abstract policy question.

The preliminary result was encouraging. Compared with applicants who were not granted membership or did not use it, people who gained membership and visited a pantry experienced an estimated 15.9-percentage-point reduction in food insecurity. The reported 95 per cent confidence interval ranged from a reduction of 29.7 points to a reduction of 2.23 points. Put simply, the estimated association was substantial, although the range of plausible effects was wide.

There are several reasons to interpret that finding carefully. This was a quasi-experimental comparison, and gaining membership is not identical to using it. People who visit a pantry may differ in motivation, circumstances or immediate needs from those who do not. Fixed-effects regression helps account for persistent differences between people, but cannot automatically remove every possible time-varying source of bias. The conference abstract calls the estimates preliminary, and a fuller paper may refine them.

Even with those cautions, the study addresses an important practical issue. Policymakers and charities often need to decide whether to support community retail models alongside emergency food assistance. The relevant question is not whether pantry shopping sounds dignified or appealing, but whether it improves material conditions for households facing hardship. Measuring outcomes over time is a step towards answering that question.

The authors also plan to examine mental wellbeing and social outcomes. That matters because reliable access to food can affect far more than nutrition: it may influence stress, household routines and the ability to participate in community life. The available abstract does not establish those additional benefits, however, and they should not be assumed from the headline food insecurity finding.

The larger lesson is methodological as well as social. Evaluating food interventions in realistic settings is difficult, especially where people cannot ethically be denied help simply for research purposes. Waiting lists and variation in actual participation create opportunities to learn, but require honest discussion of uncertainty. The preliminary evidence suggests community pantries may help; stronger conclusions depend on the detailed follow-up analysis and replication elsewhere.
qualitative-process: A clever intervention can work perfectly in theory and still disappear into the background of everyday life. That is particularly true of online grocery shopping. People arrive with shopping lists, budgets and habits; a pop-up offering a greener choice must compete for attention with all three. A qualitative study of an online supermarket intervention asks what happens between the research design and the moment a real shopper decides what to buy.

The intervention combined two ideas. Products could carry environmental labels, and shoppers could be offered more sustainable alternatives, sometimes with a price discount. Both mechanisms seem intuitive: information helps consumers identify environmentally preferable products, while lower prices make switching easier. But the actual experience depends on whether people notice the tools, understand them and find the suggested products acceptable substitutes.

Researchers interviewed 24 recipients and four people involved in implementing the intervention. The interviews explored purchasing choices, the perceived effects of the tools, and the practical processes that enabled or obstructed implementation. The study used a qualitative, thematic analysis informed by realist principles. It was therefore designed to explain experiences and possible mechanisms, not to estimate a population-wide treatment effect.

Shoppers described several obstacles to engagement. Some did not fully understand the intervention or had limited exposure to it. Their knowledge about health and sustainability varied, as did the weight they placed on those aims relative to affordability, quality and similarity to their usual purchases. A product can carry a better environmental rating and still be an unattractive substitute for someone planning a specific meal.

Habits also mattered. People who shop regularly online may respond differently from people who mostly shop in stores. Interviewees suggested that effectiveness could vary across households and shopping routines. These observations are useful because interventions that perform well in a technically proficient or motivated sample may not transfer unchanged to a broader population.

The implementers highlighted a different type of obstacle: technology. Browser extensions interacting with supermarket websites require specialist development skills, and those websites change. A small modification to a retailer's interface can create unforeseen technical problems. Existing software components and adequate technical and financial resources made implementation easier. None of this would necessarily appear in a conventional chart showing average purchasing outcomes.

There were also subtler reactions. Both recipients and implementers believed the intervention could work by nudging consumers and adding information. Some shoppers mentioned guilt about choosing less sustainable products. That reaction might change behaviour for some people, but it raises a separate question about how environmental information is communicated. An intervention can influence people psychologically without necessarily making shopping more convenient or pleasant.

Participants suggested improving usability and finding ways to publicise the tools more effectively. The implementers emphasised that large-scale improvements in food systems ultimately require policy action, not just isolated consumer-facing features. This is a perspective expressed in interviews, not an impact estimate produced by the study, but it is an important distinction for translating research into policy.

The study's value lies in showing why an apparently simple digital intervention is not simple at all. Prices, habits, product preferences, digital literacy and website design all shape what consumers can do. The conference abstract concludes that the intervention was considered acceptable and potentially useful, while identifying opportunities to improve and scale it. A process evaluation cannot say on its own how much greener shoppers' baskets became. It can help explain why future trials may succeed or fail.
ecolabel-abstract: Imagine two ways to encourage a greener grocery basket. One puts a simple environmental rating next to products, telling shoppers which options are more sustainable. The other offers a modest price reduction for choosing a greener alternative. Which approach changes what people actually buy? A randomised online supermarket trial brings evidence to a debate often dominated by assumptions about consumer awareness and willingness to pay.

The researchers studied real purchases on a UK supermarket website using a specially designed browser extension. This matters because people may express strong environmental preferences in a survey, but shopping involves immediate trade-offs over prices, tastes, familiar brands and time. Observing purchases offers a different test from asking shoppers what they intend to do.

The trial used a two-by-three factorial design. Participants were randomly allocated between seeing environmental labels or not, and between offers of a £1 discount, a 50p discount or no discount on suggested sustainable substitutes. Eco-labels graded products from A, the best environmental performance, to G, the worst. The suggested replacement products had to be more sustainable and at least as good nutritionally according to traffic-light information, and were generally priced within £2 of the original.

The primary outcome was the average eco-score of purchased goods, with a lower score meaning a greener basket. The conference abstract reported preliminary analyses of 1,431 participants enrolled in five recruitment waves between April and November 2024 who completed more than one shop during an eight-week study period. The trial was still collecting further data at the time covered by that abstract.

The first clear result was that eco-labels alone showed negligible impact on average purchasing sustainability. The estimated coefficient was 0.04, with a standard error of 0.43 and a p-value of 0.92. Within the precision of this preliminary analysis, giving shoppers environmental information in that form did not noticeably improve the score of their purchases.

Discounts looked more promising, especially at the larger amount. For a £1 discount, the estimated coefficient was minus 0.90, with a standard error of 0.49 and a p-value of 0.07. This provides suggestive, rather than conventionally decisive, evidence that financially rewarding the sustainable alternative can reduce the environmental score of the basket.

The researchers also reported a possible interaction between labels and discounts. The discount effect appeared greater when shoppers also saw eco-labels, with an interaction estimate of minus 1.53 and a p-value of 0.03. This raises an interesting possibility: labels might be more useful when combined with a reason to act. But interaction results deserve careful reading, particularly in a multi-arm trial and when the reported analysis is preliminary.

The mechanisms matter as much as the overall effect. A discount may make a substitute cheaper, draw attention to it or simply encourage the shopper to examine something unfamiliar. An eco-label may help someone understand why a product was suggested. The abstract notes that later work would explore swap acceptance and willingness to pay, as well as possible nutritional implications. The preliminary results alone cannot tell us precisely which psychological mechanism dominated.

What should policymakers take away? The evidence suggests that simply displaying information may be insufficient to shift established purchasing patterns. Incentives can be more effective, though their design and cost matter. The conference authors suggest that taxes and subsidies may have a greater impact than information-only policies. That is a plausible policy implication, not a direct estimate of a nationwide subsidy programme. The careful conclusion is that sustainable choices depend on both knowledge and the economic conditions under which people shop.
house-of-lords: What would it take to make healthier eating genuinely affordable? The question often becomes a contest between two explanations of poor diets. One emphasises what individuals choose to buy and eat; the other looks at the circumstances that shape the options available to them. In written evidence to a House of Lords committee examining food, diet and obesity, economist Thijs van Rens argued that government should take the second explanation seriously, particularly when markets deliver distorted food prices.

The submission was addressed to the Food, Diet and Obesity Committee and concerned policy tools for preventing obesity, including the role of the food and drink industry. It drew on research with Warwick economists Roberto Pancrazi and Marija Vukotic. Rather than beginning with advice on how individuals should behave, it asked a basic economic question: are prices giving people the right incentives to eat well?

Prices are sometimes described as neutral facts that consumers must work around. Economists treat them as signals, reflecting costs, competition, production practices and government policy. If those signals are distorted, a person's apparently voluntary decision may not yield the best outcome for their health or for society. The submission argues that correcting such distortions could improve diets rapidly and sustainably.

The distinction matters because simple appeals to personal responsibility can miss constraints that people cannot easily change. Someone with plenty of money, time and nearby shops faces a different set of choices from a household under financial pressure in an area with fewer good food options. The same stated preference for a healthy diet could lead to very different baskets when budgets and availability differ.

The submission builds on an earlier intervention to a House of Commons health committee in 2018 that focused on health taxes. In the later House of Lords evidence, van Rens makes a particular case for subsidies. A tax makes an undesirable choice more expensive. A subsidy makes an encouraged choice cheaper. Both change relative prices, but their distributional effects and their public reception may differ substantially.

The evidence presents subsidies as a potentially more acceptable and less intrusive way to intervene. A subsidy does not prohibit a food or compel a purchase; it changes the financial conditions under which people choose. That argument is especially pertinent when the problem is not a lack of information, but the relative cost of healthier foods. A price reduction can also matter to people who already know which foods they would like to eat more often.

Still, the existence of a promising economic rationale does not mean any subsidy will work. The precise products subsidised, the size of the incentive, retailer responses and the way a policy is funded can all affect its impact. Whether consumers switch purchases rather than simply spending less on what they would have bought anyway is an empirical question. Those details need investigation rather than assumption.

There is also a broader question of political legitimacy. Nutrition policy is often criticised as paternalistic because it seeks to influence intimate daily decisions. A price-based approach does influence choices, but so do existing food prices, marketing and product placement. The relevant debate is therefore not whether decisions are influenced, but which influences public policy should correct, and who benefits from doing so.

This piece of evidence is a policy submission, not a new randomised trial with a single headline treatment effect. Its importance lies in connecting economic reasoning to the practical options facing government. The proposition is straightforward: if unhealthy diets partly reflect a food environment shaped by distorted incentives, changing those incentives may do more than repeatedly telling consumers to choose differently.
springer-field-trial: When people say they want to eat more sustainably, researchers face a problem: what they say in a questionnaire is not necessarily what they buy at the supermarket. Shopping involves familiar brands, favourite recipes, a weekly budget and choices made in a hurry. In a research article introducing the SALIENT Sustained trial, Thijs van Rens and Oyinlola Oyebode explain how they planned to study sustainable food choices in that everyday setting rather than in an artificial shopping experiment.

The idea is to observe and intervene in real online grocery shopping. Online shopping accounted for about 12 per cent of the UK grocery market at the time the article was written, making it a substantial setting in its own right. It also allows researchers to introduce changes to what shoppers see, while observing subsequent purchases. The trial uses a purpose-built browser extension on a major UK supermarket website.

Two interventions are central. The first is an environmental label, grading products from A to G according to their estimated environmental impact. The labels are based on life-cycle assessments, which seek to measure impacts across a product's supply chain rather than just at the checkout. In principle, a label offers consumers a simple way to identify more sustainable options without having to research the footprint of every ingredient.

The second intervention tackles prices. When shoppers put particular items in their basket, the extension can propose more sustainable substitutes. For example, a plant-based yoghurt might be suggested in place of a conventional one. Some participants are offered a 50p or £1 discount on the replacement. That creates an opportunity to test whether an attractive price can help people move beyond habitual purchases.

The distinction between these tools matters. Information can tell someone which product has the lower estimated environmental impact, but that person may still prefer the cheaper or more familiar item. A discount changes the trade-off. Studying both interventions, separately and together, offers a way to see whether giving people information works better when the suggested alternative is also financially appealing.

Participants were to be recruited from Prolific and would need to shop online regularly and be a primary grocery shopper in their household. They would install the extension and shop over an eight-week period. The system would record the products they bought, allowing analysis of their baskets rather than solely their reported intentions. The authors also planned to examine nutritional quality, recognising that environmental and health objectives do not always coincide perfectly.

The article describes an adaptive trial design: researchers could adjust recruitment between waves in response to early statistical evidence. Such an approach can use research resources more efficiently, but it also makes careful documentation of procedures and outcomes important. This was a description of a trial under way, not a report establishing its eventual results.

An especially interesting feature is the relationship with supermarkets. Much research into retail behaviour depends on retailers agreeing to share data or implement interventions. Here, the extension gives researchers a different route, with shoppers participating directly. That could make it possible to evaluate interventions even when a supermarket does not itself collaborate, although technical changes to retail websites remain a practical challenge.

The broader ambition is to move beyond debates about what consumers claim to value and study what happens when conditions change in the real marketplace. The authors hope this can inform policies for healthier diets and lower environmental impacts. But an account written before the trial results must be read as a research plan, not proof that either labels or discounts succeed. The value of the design lies in creating a credible test of precisely those questions.
sky-food-industry: Why do some of the easiest foods to buy make healthy eating more difficult? A Sky News investigation into Britain's food industry raises that question through interviews with researchers, consumers and industry representatives. Economist Thijs van Rens contributes an explanation rooted in the economics of processing and pricing: the food system is organised to make particular products cheap, convenient and profitable, and those incentives can conflict with public health.

Manufacturing and processing can substantially reduce the cost of storing, transporting and selling food. Products with a long shelf life are easier to distribute and less likely to be wasted before they reach a shopper. Processing can involve adding salt, sugar or preservatives and removing ingredients that complicate storage or production. These changes can be attractive commercially, even where they are not beneficial for nutrition.

The investigation describes how manufacturers also have an incentive to sell more of their products. That is not an accusation that every business behaves identically. It is a feature of competitive markets: producers seek lower costs and stronger demand. When demand is influenced by taste, convenience and marketing, the cheapest route to commercial success is not necessarily the route that improves the country's overall diet.

The report draws attention to a stark comparison from the Food Foundation: products higher in sugar, salt and fat cost £4.30 per thousand calories on average, compared with £8.80 for healthier alternatives. Such averages do not mean every processed food is unhealthy or every healthy meal expensive. They do, however, illustrate how the price of calories can affect the options that appear realistic to households shopping on tight budgets.

The story also shows why financial comparisons alone are incomplete. One interviewee describes substantially higher grocery spending after trying to improve her diet. Other people interviewed say fresh home cooking can be affordable. Those experiences are not necessarily contradictory. Families differ in kitchen facilities, local shops, cooking skills, household preferences and how much time they have outside paid work.

Van Rens highlights time poverty alongside income poverty. People working long hours, juggling multiple jobs or caring for children may have little opportunity to prepare meals from scratch. A convenient processed option can be rational in the circumstances, even if it is less healthy. Telling people simply to cook more overlooks that time is itself a scarce economic resource.

The article also links the price and convenience of food to inequalities in health. When healthier options require extra money or preparation time, the consequences are unlikely to be distributed evenly. The report cites evidence of stark differences in obesity and related health outcomes across socioeconomic groups. Those differences should not be reduced to claims that lower-income families care less about nutrition.

There is an important counterargument in the investigation. The Food and Drink Federation points to regulation and nutritional labelling and says its members have reduced contributions of calories, sugar and salt to the grocery market over time. That response matters: industry practices change, and sweeping accounts of food companies as uniformly harmful cannot substitute for measurement. The central policy question concerns the overall incentives created by production, retail and regulation.

This is journalistic reporting with interviews and figures from several sources, not a single controlled scientific study. Its distinctive contribution is to make an economic argument tangible. The cost of food is not only the price on a shelf. It includes the time required to prepare a meal and, potentially, health costs borne later by individuals and society. Any serious debate about making diets healthier must address all three.
salient-oxford: Imagine entering a supermarket where the healthier, greener choice is also the easier choice. You don't need to research emissions during the weekly shop or navigate a jungle of competing labels. Better information is at hand, more sustainable alternatives are easy to spot, and prices don't punish you for choosing them. That is the appealing possibility behind an Oxford University feature on the SALIENT food trials, published in July 2026.

The feature asks a practical question: what if healthier, greener eating were cheaper and easier? Oxford's public summary says trials in real-world food settings show that making healthier and more sustainable choices cheaper and more accessible can improve what people eat. It is a useful framing because diet change is often portrayed as an entirely individual responsibility, when the supermarket and the wider food environment shape what feels possible.

A particularly revealing part of the programme is the SALIENT Sustained online grocery experiment, led by Warwick economist Thijs van Rens with collaborators. A browser extension introduced environmental ratings alongside foods offered by a major UK online supermarket. It also suggested alternative products with lower environmental impacts; in some cases these substitutes came with price discounts. Rather than asking consumers what they might do in an imaginary scenario, the team followed choices in a genuine online shopping environment.

The 2026 Warwick account of this research describes an eight-week randomised controlled trial involving 1,835 UK online grocery shoppers. Its headline finding is that a discount of up to £1 on more sustainable substitute products could move purchasing towards greener food. Environmental labels by themselves had much less influence. When labels accompanied price incentives, however, they could help shoppers recognise what the offer was trying to achieve. This distinction matters: knowing that one food has a smaller footprint does not necessarily outweigh price, habit or the needs of a household meal.

Why experiment with online shopping? Because its structure creates an unusually direct opportunity to test interventions. Products can be rated, swaps can appear just when a customer makes a purchasing decision, and the response can be observed in real transactions rather than recalled later. It also makes the limits of the approach visible: not every alternative suits a recipe, a budget or a family's preferences. A well-intentioned nudge can easily become another annoying obstacle if it fails to respect those constraints.

The broader SALIENT agenda stretches beyond one browser extension. The underlying policy question is how the environments in which we buy and eat food can be redesigned so that healthy and sustainable choices become ordinary, rather than exceptional. Sometimes information helps. Sometimes relative prices matter more. And sometimes convenience, availability and the format of an offer may decide whether a change happens at all.

There are important limits to what the available evidence establishes. The Warwick trial tests a particular set of interventions in one UK online grocery setting; it is not proof that every subsidy, label or product swap would work equally well elsewhere. The Oxford feature presents a programme-level story, whereas the concrete trial details here come from Warwick's separate March 2026 report. Broader policies will need tests across more shopping environments and different groups of consumers.

Still, the central insight is both simple and consequential. A food system that leaves customers to carry all the effort of changing diets is unlikely to move fast enough. If information, alternatives and prices work together, the next healthier and greener meal may require less personal resolve and more thoughtful design. The challenge is to find interventions that are effective, affordable and fair—and to test them where food decisions really happen.
plate-to-planet: A decision made in front of a supermarket shelf can seem almost comically small beside the climate crisis. Chicken or beans? A familiar ready meal or an alternative? Yet scale up those decisions across millions of households, and dinner becomes an important part of the story of emissions, agricultural land, public health and economic policy. That is the territory of Warwick's research impact feature, *From plate to planet*.

The Warwick page introduces the work of economist Thijs van Rens as an effort to tackle obesity and the climate crisis together. The pairing is deliberate. Food policy often treats poor health and environmental damage as separate problems, even though both are partly shaped by the same production systems, retail practices and dietary habits. An intervention that changes what people buy might plausibly improve both outcomes—but it needs testing, not just good intentions.

The scale of the challenge helps explain why food features so prominently in climate debates. Producing meals requires land, energy, fertiliser, transport and processing. Ruminant livestock also generates methane, a particularly potent greenhouse gas. Not every food has the same environmental footprint, and broad categories conceal substantial variation. The interesting policy question is therefore not just whether people should eat differently, but how to make lower-impact choices appealing and feasible across the food system.

This is where economics enters. When shoppers choose a product, they compare its price, familiarity, convenience and expected taste. Its environmental footprint is rarely visible in the same way. Even highly motivated consumers can struggle to interpret impact information, and households face real financial constraints. Simply telling people to be greener ignores the forces that shape the checkout basket. To change aggregate behaviour, researchers need to understand incentives and how readily one food can substitute for another.

A concrete example comes from the SALIENT Sustained online supermarket trial described by Warwick in March 2026. Researchers tested environmental labels and offers of lower-impact product alternatives, sometimes including discounts. In the eight-week study, involving 1,835 UK online shoppers, discounted swaps produced measurable movement toward more sustainable baskets. The public report emphasised that information alone was less effective. The result does not imply that every food choice is easily changed; rather, it points to the importance of presenting an acceptable alternative at a price people can afford.

Research tools are part of the story too. The THRIVING Food Futures project brings researchers together to design and evaluate interventions in real food settings. Warwick's March 2025 description explains that the programme includes nutritional and environmental profiling tools and digital systems that let research teams investigate food purchasing on supermarket and delivery platforms. These instruments can help bridge a persistent gap between laboratory-style intentions and purchasing behaviour in everyday life.

One temptation is to turn this into a story of guilt: the planet is in trouble, and the individual at the checkout must do better. But the research points in a different direction. Retailers choose which goods to stock and promote. Policymakers influence relative prices and information standards. Producers determine what alternatives exist. Customers retain agency, but they make decisions within a system whose rules and incentives are not of their own making.

There are caveats. The Warwick impact page is a broad introduction rather than a detailed scientific report, and the specific figures cited here are drawn from Warwick's separate accounts of the Sustained trial and the THRIVING programme. No one experiment establishes an entire national food strategy. Changes that work online may operate differently in a shop aisle, school canteen or takeaway app. Equity matters too: a greener food environment should not be designed on the assumption that everyone can pay more.

What the plate-to-planet perspective offers is a way to connect seemingly private decisions to public outcomes without treating consumers as the sole source of the problem. The ambitious goal is not to lecture people about their dinners. It is to build and rigorously evaluate a food system in which eating well for ourselves and the planet becomes easier to do.
food-podcast: If the future of food is greener, healthier and fairer, what will it actually look like in the supermarket on a Tuesday evening? That question runs through an episode of Wellcome's *When Science Finds a Way*, titled *Food for thought: eating our way to a sustainable future*. Host Alisha Wainwright speaks to Oxford researcher Pete Scarborough and hears from Jo, a shopper testing a tool designed to make more sustainable choices visible as she buys groceries online.

The episode begins with the scale of the problem. Food production accounts for a substantial share of greenhouse gas emissions, while also contributing to land pressure, biodiversity loss and pollution. Scarborough explains why animal-source foods—especially meat from ruminant animals—tend to have larger environmental impacts than many plant foods. The point is not that every person must adopt an identical menu. Even relatively modest reductions in meat consumption can reduce a diet's footprint.

That observation leads to a deeper challenge. Scientists have become considerably better at estimating the health and environmental consequences of diets. Scarborough describes work linking ingredient and agricultural data so researchers can estimate the footprints of tens of thousands of supermarket products. But translating that knowledge into actual shopping decisions is another problem entirely. People do not select food by reading academic tables. They select it under time pressure, with price tags, family preferences and familiar meals in mind.

At about thirteen minutes into the episode, the focus shifts to Sustained, an online supermarket trial led by Warwick economist Thijs van Rens. A browser extension places environmental ratings alongside products and offers lower-impact swaps at checkout, sometimes with discounts. It is an attempt to bring research to the point of purchase instead of expecting shoppers to search out the information themselves.

Jo's experience gives the trial a human dimension. She describes the ratings as a way of making the differences among foods immediately visible. She wants to make more meat-free meals, but also has to think about whether her children will eat them and whether the substitute suits a planned recipe. She recalls accepting a swap when the price difference was manageable and the alternative would not spoil the meal. This is not a story of someone being transformed overnight. It is an account of small choices becoming more thinkable when the necessary information appears at the right moment.

The podcast also explores the limits of universal dietary advice. Its description highlights how guidance developed in wealthy Western settings may not transfer neatly to every culture or country. Diets have different meanings, food traditions and practical constraints. A policy that treats eating as a purely technical question of nutrients and emissions could neglect those differences, and may fail for that reason alone.

The wider research programme, Scarborough explains, attempts to co-design possible policies with the public, policymakers and the food industry, then evaluate them in real settings. That sequence matters. An elegant intervention is of little use if retailers will not implement it, shoppers reject it or its outcomes are not measurable. The podcast's message is pragmatic: learn what can change, test whether it changes, and distinguish promising mechanisms from attractive slogans.

Listeners should also keep the evidential categories straight. Jo is one participant describing her experience, not a statistical estimate of the trial's effect. The episode explains the intervention and the everyday barriers it confronts; quantitative conclusions require the trial's published findings. As a piece of science communication, however, the conversation makes a crucial issue tangible. Sustainable eating is not only about knowing what is better. It is about what becomes possible when information, price and convenience line up with the demands of an ordinary household.
publication-cd2d107090c0: Food choices made at the grocery store have a profound impact on personal health and wellbeing. Recognising this, researchers have increasingly explored ‘food swap’ interventions — strategies that encourage consumers to swap less healthy items for healthier alternatives during shopping. A recent systematic review examined the evidence on how such interventions are designed and how effective they have been at changing behaviour when tested both online and in physical stores.

The review, which included 11 studies conducted between 2006 and 2024, searched through databases including MEDLINE, Scopus, and Web of Science. The goal was to identify trials where food swap interventions were implemented specifically in grocery retail settings. These studies primarily targeted adults responsible, fully or in part, for their household’s food shopping, positioning the intervention at the decision-making moment within natural shopping environments.

Of the studies examined, one took place in an actual grocery store, three in real online supermarkets, while the remaining seven were conducted in simulated online supermarket environments. Across them all, the core approach was consistent: when a shopper selected an item identified as less healthy, they were offered a choice to swap it out for a healthier alternative. This real-time nudging aimed to improve the overall nutritional quality of the shopper’s basket.

The outcomes monitored gave insight into how well these swaps worked at encouraging healthier purchases. Key metrics included the nutritional profile of the shopping basket — looking at total energy (calories), saturated fatty acid (SFA) content, salt and sodium levels, and sugar content. These indicators serve as proxies for the healthiness of the food selected and by extension, can influence longer-term diet quality and health risks.

Results showed promising signs: ten of the eleven studies reported evidence that food swap interventions could meaningfully alter behaviour. Two studies demonstrated statistically significant improvements in overall nutritional quality of purchases. Several studies found reductions in salt or sodium content, with two reporting these outcomes. Sugar content reductions were observed in one study but were not replicated in another, suggesting variations depending on the implementation context or target group.

Additionally, multiple studies revealed significant decreases in energy content or density and saturated fat purchases, factors closely linked to obesity and cardiovascular risk. These findings indicate food swaps can encourage consumers to select options that may support healthier diets, although the degree of impact varied across studies.

While the evidence supports food swaps as a valuable public health tool, the review noted an important gap: none of the studies addressed using swaps to promote sustainable food choices, such as prioritising environmentally friendly or climate-conscious options. Given rising concerns over food system impacts on the planet, this represents a promising avenue for future research and intervention development.

The review’s authors also highlighted that most evidence comes from controlled or simulated settings, with few real-world trials in physical or online grocery stores. Expanding research in naturalistic environments would be important to understand the practical challenges and benefits when adopted by retailers and consumers at scale.

In summary, food swap interventions have demonstrated effectiveness in improving the nutritional quality of grocery shopping baskets, particularly by reducing saturated fats, sodium, and energy intake through healthier substitutions. As grocery shopping continues to evolve alongside digital technologies, integrating such nudges could become a scalable approach to support healthier eating habits at the population level.

However, further research should explore how this approach might be adapted to also support sustainable and environmentally responsible food choices. Crossing the domains of personal health and planetary health through smarter shopping guidance may be the next frontier in food swap innovation.
publication-8db8b5aaf7d7: Food insecurity remains a pressing issue in the UK, with many households unable to access enough nutritious food regularly. Community food shops, offering affordable and healthy options via a membership system, have expanded rapidly but evidence of their impact on food security and diet quality has been limited. A new study set in England now sheds light on these effects, focusing on Your Local Pantry (YLP), a nationwide network of such shops operating on a pay-per-use model.

Researchers conducted a quasi-experimental study between February and August 2025 involving adults applying to join YLP. New applications were processed based on capacity, with some applicants immediately gaining membership while others were placed on a waitlist. This waiting list created a natural experiment allowing comparison between those with and without access to the Pantries. Participants completed surveys measuring food insecurity and dietary quality at baseline, followed by assessments at 2, 6, and 10 weeks.

Food insecurity was measured using the Food and Agriculture Organization’s 8-item Food Insecurity Experience Scale, categorising participants by levels of insecurity over the two weeks prior. Dietary quality was assessed through a 14-item food frequency questionnaire producing a standardised continuous score. The study included 189 eligible adults from 76 pantries, mostly working age (around 99%), predominantly women (77%), and largely white ethnicity (75%), with over half having children.

At the start, the prevalence of food insecurity was alarmingly high: 82% experienced moderate to severe insecurity, and 48% severe food insecurity. The average diet quality score was 1.53 on a scale from 1.08 to 1.89, showing some room for improvement in their eating habits. These baseline figures highlight the challenging circumstances faced by applicants to this community food shop network.

The study's main findings were that gaining YLP membership led to a significant reduction in food insecurity compared to those who remained on the waitlist. Specifically, membership was associated with a 13.4 percentage point decrease in moderate to severe food insecurity and a 17.5 percentage point reduction in severe food insecurity. These figures indicate a substantial improvement in food access for new members.

Furthermore, the frequency of visits to YLP pantries was important. Each additional visit was linked to a further 2.4 percentage point decrease in severe food insecurity. Regarding dietary quality, while simply gaining membership was not linked to an immediate change, more frequent use of the pantries was associated with modest improvements in diet quality scores, indicating that regular engagement could support healthier eating.

This research provides some of the first strong evidence that community food shops operating on a pay-per-use membership model can effectively reduce food insecurity in adults. The association between repeated visits and improved diet quality is also encouraging, suggesting that these shops may not only alleviate hunger but also encourage better nutritional choices over time.

Nevertheless, the study acknowledges that improvements in diet quality were smaller than reductions in food insecurity, implying that while access to affordable healthy food is necessary, it may not be sufficient alone to radically change dietary habits. Further strategies might be needed to support sustained nutritional improvements among users.

Overall, the findings from Your Local Pantry offer valuable insights for policymakers and public health advocates seeking practical interventions against food poverty in the UK. Investing in community food shops and facilitating easier access could be a promising approach to improving the wellbeing of vulnerable populations, particularly families facing economic hardship.

Future research could build on these results by exploring long-term outcomes of pantry membership, impacts on children’s nutrition, or the role of complementary education and cooking support programs. Understanding how best to maximise the health benefits of such community food initiatives remains a vital goal.
publication-83528c156f8d: With online grocery shopping gaining momentum across the UK, there’s growing interest in encouraging shoppers to make not only healthier but also more environmentally friendly food choices. However, knowing which strategies actually work to guide sustainable shopping remains a challenge. A recent pilot trial set out to test whether eco-labels—simple scores rating the environmental impact of products—can influence the foods people add to their virtual baskets.

The study, conducted in late 2023, involved a browser extension integrated with a real UK supermarket website. This technology allowed researchers to track participants’ shopping in real time and display eco-labels during the intervention phase, while also collecting precise data on their purchasing behaviour. Participants were randomly allocated to two groups: one that saw eco-labels on products and another that did not.

These eco-labels scored food items from A to G, with A representing the lowest environmental impact and G the highest. For example, a plant-based item might receive an A, while heavily processed or resource-intensive foods could be rated lower. The aim was to gently prompt buyers to favour greener options.

The study was designed to first collect baseline shopping data over two weeks, with no eco-labels shown to either group, followed by a two-week intervention where only the experimental group saw the eco-labels. This approach helped isolate any changes attributable to the labels themselves.

Out of over 500 people screened, 161 met the study criteria and were invited to participate. However, only 57 downloaded the browser extension required to take part—much lower than hoped. This low uptake meant the researchers had limited data to detect meaningful differences in shopping behaviour between groups.

When analysing the results, the average eco-scores of shopping baskets in the intervention group (who saw the labels) were 41 compared to 32 in the control group. Although this difference suggests a trend towards greener purchases among the intervention group, statistical tests showed it was not significant (p = 0.22). Given the small sample size, the study cannot confidently claim that eco-labels influenced behaviour in this pilot.

Importantly, the pilot also provided valuable lessons on improving future trials. Participants reported needing more technical assistance with the browser extension, regular reminders to encourage continued use, better incentives, and clearer information about what the eco-labels meant and why they mattered.

These insights are crucial. Online shopping environments can be complicated, and simply providing information is rarely enough to change habits without supportive measures to engage users effectively. The pilot illustrates that to scale such interventions successfully, developers must prioritise user-friendly tools and motivational strategies.

The researchers plan a larger, more robust trial informed by these findings. With better recruitment, improved technology support, and enhanced communication about the benefits of eco-labels, they hope to more clearly understand whether such labels can steer consumers towards purchasing foods with lower environmental footprints.

As the UK and other countries aim to reduce the carbon impact of diets—given that food production contributes significantly to greenhouse gas emissions—tools like eco-labels could become important parts of the solution. However, digital initiatives must be carefully designed with the shopper’s experience in mind to be truly effective.

In summary, while this early investigation didn’t provide definitive proof that eco-labels drive greener grocery shopping online, it represents a promising step forward. The real-world trial approach and direct shopper feedback highlight both the potential and the practical challenges of nudging consumers towards sustainability in the digital age.
publication-505365829647: The idea that a mismatch between workers’ skills and job requirements causes economic dysfunction is widely accepted. Governments and experts agree that improving the alignment of skills supply and demand could boost productivity and reduce unemployment. The common approach has been to focus mostly on the supply side, meaning worker education and training. But recent research suggests this focus misses a key element: employers’ role in rigid and sometimes restrictive job requirements.

Skills mismatch occurs when workers either have too few or the wrong type of skills for the jobs available—or, conversely, when employees are overqualified. This mismatch dampens productivity at the individual level and can contribute to higher unemployment. For example, in OECD countries, about 35% of workers are mismatched by qualification levels, with approximately 22% over-qualified and 12% under-qualified for their jobs. Under-education is a particular challenge in lower-income countries, where up to 70% of workers may lack the necessary qualifications.

Despite evidence that individual productivity suffers when workers are mismatched, understanding the full impact on overall economic productivity is more complex. Studies estimate that in the US, the aggregate output loss linked to skills mismatch is about 7%. This figure accounts for both the reduced efficiency of under-skilled workers and the opportunity cost of overqualified employees not utilizing their full capabilities.

Skills mismatch also contributes to unemployment. If workers lack the right skills for available jobs, they remain unemployed even when vacancies exist. Studies show that one-third of the increase in unemployment during the US Great Recession was due to skills mismatch across occupations. What’s more, mismatch unemployment tends to rise during recessions, even though geographic mismatch—workers being in the wrong location relative to job openings—has minimal overall impact on unemployment levels.

Why does the skills gap persist despite workers adapting to changing economic demands? A key insight is that while supply-side adjustments like retraining are important, the demand side—in particular, how employers screen and define job requirements—is critical. Firms may have roles that they consider non-substitutable or demand particular experience, making it difficult for otherwise qualified candidates to secure employment. Overly restrictive criteria, such as insisting on specific degrees or prior experience unrelated to the essential skills, can exacerbate mismatch problems.

For example, requiring an internship at a prestigious organisation as a prerequisite for entry-level roles can exclude capable candidates. Automated screening systems may also filter out potential hires prematurely. This inflexibility means that even when workers develop relevant skills, they may face barriers to employment if companies maintain rigid hiring practices.

This understanding challenges the widespread assumption that the solution lies solely in enhancing education and training systems. While improving skills remains valuable, policies ignoring employers’ hiring behaviours may fall short. Expensive reforms to education without addressing demand-side rigidities might increase the number of “qualified” candidates yet fail to reduce mismatch or unemployment.

Additionally, recent research on the impact of artificial intelligence on jobs found no clear overall reduction in employment or wages, suggesting that technological change alone does not fully explain persistent mismatch. Instead, labour market segmentation, job-substitution limits, and recruitment frictions remain significant obstacles.

Measurement complexities remain a challenge. Skills mismatch is multi-dimensional—technical, cognitive, and soft skills all matter, as do industry-specific knowledge and personality traits. Data reliance on occupational classifications or self-reported skills has limitations. Moreover, defining appropriate labour market segments to measure mismatch and quantify its effects accurately is difficult. This underscores the need for nuanced approaches and better data to inform policy.

In summary, effectively addressing the skills mismatch and its economic consequences requires a balanced view. Worker education and training are important, but employers must also be encouraged to adopt flexible, realistic hiring criteria that recognise transferable skills and potential. Without tackling both supply and demand-side factors, the persistent skills gap and associated costs in productivity and unemployment will likely endure.
publication-c136ac91d492: The COVID-19 lockdowns dramatically altered daily life in the UK, sparking widespread concerns about their impact on people’s health behaviours and overall well-being. A longitudinal study conducted in the West Midlands sheds new light on how these restrictions affected diet, physical activity, mental health, and body weight over time.

The research involved an online survey of more than 1,000 adults, with nearly 500 respondents completing two surveys: one during a strict lockdown phase and another once restrictions had mostly eased. This design allowed researchers to explore changes within the same individuals as circumstances evolved.

Focusing on fruit and vegetable intake as an indicator of a healthy diet, the study found no evidence that consumption declined during lockdown. Quite the opposite occurred for some groups, particularly women. This subgroup ate on average half a portion more fruit and vegetables each day during lockdown compared to after, suggesting an improvement rather than deterioration in dietary quality.

One key factor linked to this increase was commuting. Women who typically faced long daily commutes appeared to benefit from the extra time at home lockdown provided, enabling them to prepare and consume healthier meals. This novel insight points to the potential negative impact of commuting on diet and suggests that reduced travel time can facilitate better food choices.

Alongside dietary data, the study also measured physical activity and found a significant increase during lockdown. This pattern aligns with participants reporting higher self-perceived health, hinting at a broader shift to healthier lifestyle behaviours when freed from routine constraints such as office hours and commuting.

However, the picture was not entirely positive. Despite signs of improved diet and activity, mental well-being deteriorated markedly during lockdown periods. Participants reported increased feelings of distress or unease, echoing findings from other research highlighting lockdown’s adverse effect on mental health.

In addition, many respondents felt they had gained weight despite eating more fruit and vegetables and exercising more. This suggests complex interactions between diet, physical activity, and body weight that may involve factors not fully captured in the study, such as increased snacking or changes in eating habits beyond fruit and vegetable intake.

The qualitative part of the study explored participants’ experiences and revealed that having more time was a crucial facilitator for healthier eating, even though some faced difficulties accessing food. This abundance of time contrasts with pre-lockdown routines, showing how lifestyle constraints affect the ability to maintain a healthy diet.

Overall, this research challenges fears that lockdowns undermined diet quality and health behaviours across the board. Instead, it highlights how lifestyle flexibility, particularly reduced commuting, can positively influence healthy eating habits, especially among women.

Nevertheless, the study adds important evidence to concerns about the significant decline in mental health during lockdown, emphasizing the need for balanced approaches in future public health measures that consider both physical and psychological well-being.

These findings offer valuable insights for policymakers and public health professionals aiming to support community health during extended periods of social restrictions or remote working. Encouraging flexible working arrangements and addressing mental health could form part of strategies to promote healthier, more sustainable lifestyles in a post-pandemic world.
publication-e6c5fa2b8af5: Supermarkets frequently use promotions to boost sales, but such offers often target less healthy products like soft drinks and confectionery. A recent analysis assessed the impact of voluntarily removing volume price promotions – offers such as “buy one, get one free” – in a leading UK supermarket, with the aim of exploring whether this change could reduce household expenditure on sugary drinks and confectionery items.

Researchers used data from the Worldpanel by Numerator UK consumer panel, which records purchase behaviour from around 30,000 households. Employing a difference-in-difference methodology with two-way fixed effects, the team compared shopping patterns at the intervention supermarket against those of households shopping elsewhere, allowing them to isolate the effect of removing volume price promotions from other trends influencing purchases.

The key findings showed a statistically significant reduction in expenditure on the targeted product categories amongst households mainly shopping at the supermarket that removed volume price promotions. Specifically, total spending on soft drinks decreased by 4.7% (95% confidence interval [CI]: -6.7% to -2.6%), and expenditure on confectionery fell by 3.9% (95% CI: -5.8% to -2.1%) in comparison to households in other supermarkets that did not alter their promotions.

Looking more closely at the products that had previously been offered with volume price promotions, the declines were even larger. Spending on soft drinks that had been subject to these promotions dropped by 23.2% (95% CI: -26.0% to -17.4%), while confectionery expenditure in this category declined by 7.7% (95% CI: -12.7% to -2.3%). This suggests that the removal of such promotions substantially diminishes purchasing of specifically those deals.

Interestingly, the analysis also found that expenditure on products available through other types of discounts, such as temporary price reductions, rose during the same period. Soft drink spending related to these temporary promotions increased by 6.9% (95% CI: 4.2% to 9.8%), and confectionery spending rose by 8.4% (95% CI: 6.2% to 10.7%). This indicates that while volume price promotions declined, shoppers may have partially switched to taking advantage of other discount types.

The patterns in expenditure were mirrored in the quantities of soft drinks and confectionery purchased, reinforcing the conclusion that removing volume promotions led to lower overall consumption of these less healthy products. However, the coexistence of increases in spending on temporarily discounted items highlights that shoppers’ responses to changes in promotions can be complex.

Overall, the evidence from this study suggests that supermarket policies voluntarily removing volume price promotions can achieve moderate reductions in the purchase of soft drinks and confectionery. Nevertheless, the authors indicate that to meaningfully curb the intake of less healthy foods at a population level, such measures might need to be broadened. Specifically, a ban or restriction may be needed on a wider range of promotions beyond just volume price offers to prevent substitution effects towards other discounts.

These findings contribute useful real-world evidence to ongoing debates on how retail environments influence dietary behaviours and public health. By analysing large-scale household purchase data using robust statistical methods, the study provides a nuanced understanding of how pricing strategies affect consumer choices for commonly consumed sugary products in the UK.
publication-68f45c1caff7: With rising awareness of the environmental impact of food production alongside growing interest in healthier diets, researchers are investigating ways to influence consumer choices toward more sustainable and nutritious food options. A new study protocol has been published outlining a controlled trial that will test two interventions—eco-labelling and price discounts—within the context of online grocery shopping in major UK supermarkets accessed via Google Chrome on desktop or laptop computers.

This study intends to assess how providing consumers with information on the environmental footprint of their prospective purchases, combined with financial incentives to choose more sustainable alternatives, could potentially nudge shopping habits toward better outcomes for both human and planetary health. It represents one of the early controlled evaluations focusing on real-time decision support integrated into online food retail platforms.

The research design involves two independent adaptive randomised controlled trials conducted concurrently within the same participant population. One trial has two arms, and the other has three arms, although the overall structure is not powered to detect interactions of the interventions in a factorial design. The two main interventions under investigation are as follows:

First, an eco-labelling system will be implemented as a consumer-facing information tool. Each food product will receive an eco-score ranging from "A" (most sustainable) to "G" (least sustainable), reflecting its environmental impact. This score will be visible within a bespoke browser extension installed on participants’ shopping web pages, providing immediate feedback on the sustainability of items in their basket.

Second, the study will apply targeted price discounts to products identified as more sustainable alternatives, provided that these alternatives also have equal or better nutritional profiles compared to the original items selected by shoppers. This financial incentive aims to encourage substitution toward greener options without compromising dietary quality.

The primary outcome measure for the trials will be the average eco-score of participants’ shopping baskets, assessing any shift toward more sustainably rated products. Secondary outcomes will include analyses of the nutritional content of the shopping baskets, with health outcomes further modelled using established nutrition scoring methods. This dual focus on environmental and nutritional quality acknowledges the interconnected goals of planetary and human health.

To deliver the interventions seamlessly within usual shopping behaviours, the team will deploy a browser extension compatible with the Google Chrome web browser, facilitating real-time information and price adjustments on online grocery websites for at least one major UK supermarket chain, or potentially multiple large supermarkets.
